$comment: #1933 / UX-P111 — THE WHOLE PERCENT A SURFACE PRINTS FOR A PROBABILITY.
Ruling 021: when several consumers must agree about the same input, the unit
to share is the DECISION, not the ingredient. Three runtimes print this
number — Python on the server, TypeScript on web, Swift on native — and no
import spans them. So the shared unit is this table, and every
implementation's test drives ITS function through EVERY row here.
WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A ROUNDING RULE USUALLY DOES. The card fingerprint
that gates a graded verdict (`app/utils/graded_card.py`) is taken at this
resolution on purpose, so that it 'changes exactly when the picture changes'
and every refusal is explicable to the person who was looking at the card. If
the server rounds a card to 56 and the screen prints 57, that sentence is
false at precisely the values where it is hardest to be right — the card
would be refused for drift nobody can see, or pass while visibly different.
WHAT WENT WRONG WITHOUT IT. UX-P110 shipped `rendered_percent` using Python's
built-in `round`, which is BANKER'S rounding: `round(56.5)` is 56, while
`Math.round(56.5)` is 57. The test next to it asserted the JavaScript answer
in a comment and the Python one in the assertion, so it was green and wrong
in the same file. A comment cannot keep two runtimes honest; it kept zero.
THE RULE: floor(p * 100 + 0.5), evaluated in double precision, with the
multiply done FIRST. That is `Math.round` and Swift's default
`.rounded()` (.toNearestOrAwayFromZero) over the non-negative domain
probabilities live in, and it is deliberately NOT Python's `round`.
THE MULTIPLY-FIRST PART IS LOAD-BEARING, and the 0.565 row is why: 0.565 * 100
is 56.49999999999999 in IEEE 754, not 56.5, so the honest answer is 56 in all
three runtimes — measured, in all three. An implementation that 'fixed' this
with a decimal type would print 57 and disagree with the other two. The table
pins the arithmetic, not an idealised mathematical rounding.
TO CHANGE THE RULE: change the rows here first, watch all three suites go red,
then change the implementations.
rule: floor(probability * 100 + 0.5), IEEE 754 double, multiply before rounding; null in, null out
$card_rule_comment: VERSION 2 ADDS THE CARD-LEVEL DECISION (#2060). Getting every individual
number right is not enough, because a surface prints a CARD and a card has a
SUM. Alex's 08-20 gold session served `Los Angeles D 0.925 / Colorado 0.075`,
which this table renders as 93 and 8 — both correct, and 101 together.
Kalshi quotes a complement pair on a HALF-CENT grid, so `p * 100` lands on `.5`
for BOTH sides at once and half-up rounds both up. Measured on production
2026-08-21: 10,198 of 21,524 open two-outcome markets render a sum other than
100, and 8,982 of those are 101 against 318 at 99 — a 28:1 skew, i.e. one
systematic cause rather than noise.
THE RULE: if the card has exactly two priced outcomes summing into
[0.99, 1.01], divide both by that total, round INDEX 0 with the scalar rule
above, and derive index 1 as `100 - index0`. Otherwise render each outcome
independently and change nothing.
WHY INDEX 0 SURVIVES: it is the card's headline — what `rendered_probability`
reports and the first number a reader reads. The derived +/-1 belongs on the
side nobody is quoting.
WHY THE BAND IS [0.99, 1.01] AND NOT WIDER. Two outcomes are not automatically
two sides of one question; measured two-outcome field sums run from 0.001 to
2.0, and normalizing 0.001 would invent a probability rather than round one.
But 19,564 of 21,410 (91.4%) sit in (0.99, 1.01], and 1.01 is already this
codebase's own two-outcome 'true binary' threshold in
`card_integrity.display_scale`. So the band is that existing constant made
SYMMETRIC — and the missing lower half was itself part of the defect, since a
pair summing to 0.99 printed 99 and nothing considered that wrong.
`field_coherence`'s [0.5, 1.5] band is deliberately NOT the predicate: under it
a pair summing to 1.49 would be normalized, which is fabrication.
card_rule: exactly two priced outcomes summing into [0.99, 1.01] => normalize by the total, round index 0, derive index 1 as 100 - index0; otherwise render each independently
$swift_note: The Swift arm executes under `scripts/ios_native_gate.sh test`, which does
NOT run in CI — so its case table is inlined in the test file and the jest
contract suite asserts that table equals these rows. The runtime check runs
locally; the DRIFT check runs in CI. Putting only one of those in place is
how the Swift copy quietly stops being the same rule.
$cases_comment: Every `percent` below was COMPUTED in all three runtimes and found to agree,
not reasoned about — the row this table replaces was reasoned about and was
wrong. `discriminates` marks the rows where Python's built-in `round` gives a
DIFFERENT answer; there are five of them, and a suite that happens to omit all

`test_graded_card_contract.py` asserts that at least those five are present,
so the table cannot be quietly defanged by deleting rows.

37.5 exactly — banker's also gives 38; the pair with 0.125 shows the rule is not 'always up by one'

57.49999999999999, same reason — pinned because it LOOKS like a .5 boundary and is not

$printed_cases_comment: VERSION 5 ADDS THE PRINTED STRING (UX-P192). `rendered_percent` above is the
INTEGER. It is not what a reader sees, because an integer cannot say the one
thing a small price most needs to say. A market quoted at 0.0004 renders to
`0`, and `0%` does not read as 'unlikely' — it reads as IMPOSSIBLE, printed
over a quote a market is actively making. UX-P046 fixed that on web with the
band, and native grew its own copy of the band the same week.
THE TWO COPIES WERE NOT THE SAME FUNCTION, and nothing could have noticed,
because the band had no rows here. Web derived it from the ROUNDING RESULT
(`rounded <= 0 && p > 0`); native used two hand-picked THRESHOLDS
(`pct < 1`, `pct > 99`). They agree across most of the interval and disagree
at four places, every one of them a place where being wrong is expensive:
p = 0.005  web `1%`     native `<1%`   — four live weather buckets sat here
p = 0      web `0%`     native `<1%`   — impossible reported as merely unlikely
p = 1      web `100%`   native `>99%`  — certainty taken off a settled market
The last two are the ones that matter beyond parity: a formatter that exists
to stop a boundary being claimed falsely must not claim the INTERIOR falsely
either, and 'settled means settled' (Alex) is a product ruling, not a taste.
THE RULE, and note that it is stated over the INTEGER the rows above produce,
so the two halves of this contract cannot drift apart: print `<1%` when the
integer is <= 0 while the probability is strictly positive, `>99%` when it is
>= 100 while the probability is strictly below one, and `"{n}%"` otherwise.
A `rendered` override replaces the INTEGER and is then subject to the same
two tests, because the band is a claim about the VALUE and not about which
arithmetic produced the integer.
Python has no arm here on purpose: the server publishes numbers and the
clients print them (ruling 003). If a Python arm is ever added, it belongs in
`printed_implementations` and must be driven through every row below.
printed_rule: given r = the rendered integer (an explicit override, else floor(p*100+0.5)): '<1%' if r <= 0 and p > 0; '>99%' if r >= 100 and p < 1; otherwise '{r}%'. Non-finite p prints an em dash.

printed_cases.$why: THE ONE THAT MUST NOT BE A BAND. Exactly impossible. Native's threshold form printed `<1%` here, inventing a possibility
exactly certain. Native printed `>99%`, taking certainty off a settled market
THE EXEMPLAR — a real price rendering to 0. Both arms already agreed here; this is the row the band exists for
THE SPECIMEN — rounds half-up to 1, so it is NOT below one percent. Native's `pct < 1` said `<1%`. Four live /weather temperature buckets were priced here on 2026-08-30
0.99 rounds to 1; the threshold form banded everything under a full point
the first value both forms agreed to print plainly
the threshold was strict (`> 99`), so 99.0 exactly was the one point in that neighbourhood the two forms agreed on
rounds to 99, which is not above ninety-nine. Native printed `>99%`
rounds to 100 while strictly below 1 — the upper band's first row
the mirror of 0.0001, and the reason the band is derived from the rounding rather than from a second constant
the multiply-first row again, carried through to the string so a decimal-typed reimplementation fails here too

$printed_override_cases_comment: The `rendered` override, which is where the two halves of this contract meet.
`rendered` is the CARD-level integer the server already decided (#2060 — two
sides of one question must total 100, so neither side may round itself). It
replaces the integer and is then subject to the same two tests.
The first row is the load-bearing one: a served 100 over a probability of
0.996 still prints `>99%`, because a card-sum decision is not a licence to
claim certainty. An implementation that returned the override early — which
is exactly what native's did — passes every row above and fails this one.

printed_override_cases.$why: THE EXEMPLAR. The override cannot buy a boundary the value is not on
an ordinary override, passed straight through
#2060's own card, trailing side — 7 and not the 8 independent rounding gives
an exact one with a matching override is still plain
and an exact zero is still plain

$card_cases_comment: Every `percents` below was COMPUTED by the Python implementation and is
asserted identically by all three suites. `naive` records what INDEPENDENT
per-outcome rounding produces, and `discriminates` is true exactly where the
two disagree — those six rows are the bug. A suite that happens to omit all
six is green against the defect this rule exists for, so the Python contract
test asserts at least those six are still present.
THE NON-DISCRIMINATING ROWS ARE NOT FILLER. Four of them (0.706/0.305 summing
to 102, 0.589/0.4, 0.57/0.4 summing to 97, 0.001/0.0) are two-outcome cards
that the rule must LEAVE ALONE, and their rendered sums are deliberately not
100. A guard whose tests only prove it fires is how a diversity cap emptied
the Sports tab (gotcha #43); both directions are pinned here.

card_cases.$why: THE EXEMPLAR — #2060, market 59183794, Alex's 08-20 gold session. Independent rounding printed 93 + 8 = 101
same half-cent grid, the Angels/Astros card from the same slate
mid-field pair — the defect is not confined to lopsided cards
independent rounding printed a 100% side that was never 100%. Normalizing removes a false certainty, not just a stray point
total is 1.01 exactly — the UPPER bound is inclusive. Naive gave 102

total 0.989, just outside the lower bound — the band is closed, and one thousandth past it changes the verdict
total 0.97 — a genuinely thin book. Forcing this to 100 would claim precision the market does not have
thinnest two-outcome sum observed in production; normalizing would invent a probability rather than round one
a pair that is already consistent must stay consistent — the rule is not allowed to disturb it
three outcomes — the rule is two-outcome only and must not touch a multi-way field
one side unpriced is not a priced pair; null stays null rather than becoming a derived 40
a single outcome has no complement to derive
empty field in, empty field out

$duel_cases_comment: VERSION 3 ADDS THE DUEL — THE SAME QUESTION IN FIXED POSITIONS (UX-P114).
`card_cases` above assumes SERVED ORDER, where index 0 is the headline because
both labeling serializers sort descending before calling. The Discover EVENT
card does not sort: away is always drawn on the left, home on the right,
because those positions carry meaning a probability ranking would destroy.
It is nonetheless the most exact complement pair in the product, because
`routes/feed.py` derives the away side as `round(1.0 - current_home_prob, 6)`.
The two numbers sum to one BY CONSTRUCTION, so the defect fires on a provable
condition: whenever `home * 100` lands exactly on `.5`, both sides round up and
the card prints 101. It can never print 99. MEASURED on production 2026-08-21
over the 414 scheduled/live events inside the feed's window, blend computed by
`compute_aggregate_probability` itself: 34 (8.2%) print 101, all 101, none 99.
THE RULE: hand the FAVOURITE in at index 0 of the card rule above, then map the
result back into [away, home]. No new band, no new constant — the same
[0.99, 1.01] predicate and the same normalize-round-derive.
WHY THE FAVOURITE AND NOT THE AWAY SIDE. A duel has no served order to inherit
a headline from, so the replacement rule is the one the card rule was written to
express: the number a reader anchors on survives untouched, and the side nobody
is quoting absorbs the derived point. `positional` below records what
always-away-first would print instead, and it differs on four rows — including
Green Bay @ Denver, where it moves the FAVOURITE from its own correct 68 to 67.
That is the one number on a game card anybody checks.
Every `percents` was COMPUTED by the Python implementation. `naive` is what the
four surfaces printed before this rule (web EventCard, native DiscoverEventCard,
the macOS menu bar, and the widget — the last two re-derive `1 - home`
themselves off this very payload). The five non-discriminating rows pin the
LEAVE-ALONE direction as explicitly as the fixed one (gotcha #43).
duel_rule: render [away, home] by handing the FAVOURITE to the card rule at index 0 and mapping the result back to away/home order; a pair that is not a complement pair is rendered independently

duel_cases.$why: SPECIMEN — event 15277855, Madison Keys @ Sara Bejlek, LIVE when measured. Printed 65 + 36 = 101
SPECIMEN — event 15200290, Green Bay Packers @ Denver Broncos. Printed 33 + 68 = 101, and the row where positional derivation would move the FAVOURITE off its own correct 68
SPECIMEN — event 15197813, Toronto FC @ Inter Miami CF. A near coin flip printed 50 + 51 = 101; positional would print two 50s and lose which side is favoured
SPECIMEN — event 15176690, Lucrecia Manzur @ Amanda Serrano. The lopsided end behaves the same way
SPECIMEN — event 14897211, TSG Hoffenheim @ Erzgebirge Aue, LIVE when measured
an exact coin flip is already consistent and the rule must not disturb it
a complement pair NOT on a .5 boundary — in band, and still unchanged. This is the common case: 380 of the 414 measured events
away favourite, no boundary — the favourite-first mapping must be a no-op when nothing needs deriving
one side unpriced is not a priced pair; null stays null rather than becoming a derived 40
sum 0.9, outside the band. A game card should never produce this, but the rule must not force a total onto a pair that is not one

$card_sum_rule_comment: VERSION 4 ADDS THE REASON A CARD'S TWO NUMBERS DO NOT ADD UP (#2088).
The card rule above fixed the pair that SHOULD total 100 and deliberately left
alone the pair that should not. That was right — normalizing a pair summing to
0.97 would invent three points of probability rather than round one — but it
shipped the reader a card reading `57 / 40` with nothing on it saying why, which
is indistinguishable from the `93 / 8` bug it had just fixed. INT-104 measured
UX-P113's own deploy check at 17 of 18 and filed #2088: an UNEXPLAINED non-100
is the defect; a labelled one is a fact.
Re-measured on production 2026-08-29 over the endpoint the issue itself used:
100 cards, 18 two-outcome, 17 summing to 100, one at 99 — 'Diane Parry vs Ann
Li: Set 2 Winner', served [51, 48]. A different market from the filed exemplar
and the same shape, so the class is a population rather than an anecdote.
THE REASON IS NOT AN ILLIQUIDITY MARK, AND THAT WAS CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.
#2088 calls this 'the source-disagreement / illiquidity class', and UX-P157/158
had just built a graded mark for exactly that. On the filed exemplar
`grade_liquidity` returns 'traded': the books are 0.55/0.59 and 0.38/0.42, four
cents against a 0.57 midpoint, nowhere near `ask - bid >= midpoint`; and
`volume_updated_at` is not written on this population, so the volume fact is not
checkable either. Drawing a thinness mark here would invent a verdict that module
refuses to reach, on the surface where Alex grades. The honest reason needs no
book at all — these are two independently quoted sides, not two halves of one
question.
SCOPE: two outcomes only. A three-outcome field totalling 97 is the
independent-binary class (gotcha #23) and already has `field_coherence` and
`_feed_display_scale`. null means 'this card makes no claim about a total', never
'checked and fine' — the surfaces must not render it as a clean bill of health.
SWIFT IS DELIBERATELY NOT AN ARM. The reason is SERVED on both labeling
serializers; native consumes it rather than re-deriving it. Web implements it
only as the fallback for a payload minted before this shipped — the same role
`renderedPercent` plays for a pre-#2060 payload.
card_sum_rule: a card of exactly two outcomes whose printed percents do not total 100 carries a reason: 'unpriced_outcome' when a side has no price, otherwise 'independent_prices'; a complement pair totals 100 by construction and carries null; any arity other than two carries null

card_sum_implementations.$role: fallback for a payload minted before card_sum_reason was served
